I'm playing on PC w/ a Logitech F710 controller, and its been the best experience IMO. The mouse and keyboard controls aren't bad, and I still use my keyboard along w/ the controller, but something about the combat system does lend itself to 2 analogue sticks if you ask me.

I think you're absolutely right. Myself, I'm playing with a G13 gamepad, but am now looking to get a controller just for this game.

Can you recommend the F710 or is there a better choice to make right now?

TL;DR: Yes, however:

I used to have an Xbox 360 remote w/ the USB Wireless Windows Adapter, and it works great. If you like the way Xbox 360 (or Xbox One) controllers feel, or already have one laying around, this is totally a great option, and I can personally recommend it.

I eventually sold my Xbox 360, and the controllers along with it, so I moved on to the Logitech F710, which I Can also entirely recommend... No complaints. It takes standard AA batteries like the 360 controller, but it hasn't eaten through them any more or less than any other controller I've used that takes batteries. Just be ready for that though. If you'd rather not deal with batteries, there is the Logitech F310 which is the same controller, wired. Feels great in the hand.

I also have the nVidia Shield Controller thats made for the nVidia Shield Tablet and new Shield Console. So far (the last time i checked) it only works on PC via the USB cable (not wirelessly like it does work w/ everything else). It does use some sort of fancy custom wireless connection to be super power efficient, and low latency, so even if it did work wireless on PC, it would require a custom dongle. As far as I know there is not one, but its a GREAT controller all around... I like the way it feels more than the F710, but I like the wirelessness of the F710 so I can really kick back, so I use it (the Logitech F710) more often. nVidia Shield Controller is just for if I run out of batteries, or Player 2 :P

Outside of that, I do not have personal experience with anything else. I tried getting my PS3 Dual Shock controller working on my desktop using the custom driver people have made for it, and the bluetooth dongle I Had wasn't compatible (it only works w/ a select few bluetooth dongles, so make sure you do your research if you want to go this route). But usually these dongles are only $10-$40 depending.... If you already have a PS3/4 controller around, and like the way it feels, this might be the route to go as well... I've never done it personally, so IDK how glitchy the custom drivers are, but I know I like the way the controller feels in my hand, so I might try to get it working again some day. I just got a new bluetooth Dongle for my Raspberry Pi it might be worth trying it with. PS3/4 might be interesting to get working, but there is no official support, so you're going to be dealing with custom 3rd party drivers and settings screens, and the need for specific bluetooth dongles. Might be more trouble than its worth, but I know some people who love it.

Anyways, thats the extent of my experience. nVidia Shield controller is my favorite feel in hand, but lacks wireless on PC. Logitech F710 and Xbox 360 controller are tied for second, for feel in hand, and features. PS3/4 is wild wild west driver/settings/support wise, but also super customizable and some people can't live w/o that specific controller, they love it that much.

Another thing to consider is that most games on PC that support controllers display the xbox 360 style buttons in-game (For tutorials, etc), which the F710 mimics perfectly... so that might give those 2 controllers an edge over the rest if thats important to you.

I also have a Steam Controller preordered... who knows how well thats going to work. If I didn't have any controller I personally might be tempted to wait for that... but thats because i'm a huge Valve fanboy.

It's pretty simple!

You can submit posts. They have a title and either have a text ("Discuss" button) or link to something ("Share a link" button). When people upvoat your posts, you get points called submission contribution points, or SCP (first number on top-right after your username).

You can post comments under posts. When people upvoat your comments, you get points called comment contribution points, or CCP (second number on top-right after your username).

When you upvoat/downvoat anything, you don't get anything, but for fun you have a third number after your username which shows on how many things you've voated.

As a measure to prevent spam and mass-voating, you can only voat CCP/2 times a day. I have 282 CCP, so I can upvoat/downvoat 141 things a day. You have at least 20 (or is it 100?) voats a day though, so if your CCP is low, you can still voat.

Edit: you can also downvoat stuff only when you have 100+ CCP. Below that you can only upvoat. Above that - general rules apply: you can upvoat+downvoat CCP/2 times a day.

At the broadest level, outrage culture refers to socio-cultural factors that encourage the expression of outrage in place of the calm and rational exchange of ideas. Examples with which you are probably familiar include dogpiling, the rapid escalation of conflict, angry personal attacks, public shaming, and attempting to get people fired for expressing unpopular ideas.
